doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Melody over chord changes: Steve Wilson on Ellington, Hawkins, Bird and Stan Getz
summary: Vega argues earlier improvisers followed melodies rather than chord changes, citing Steve Wilson's Ellington story, Coleman Hawkins and Bird, and asks how Getz played Chick Corea's tunes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: By knowing, by having the amount of information in your head of what sounds right and what doesn’t sound right in the bebop tradition. Or even the blues. Understand something, up until the — I would say the inception of jazz, if you want to talk about it from 1917, if you want to talk about the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, but baloney. If we want to talk about ragtime music and improvised music coming out of New Orleans, up until even up to the 60s, by-and-large most of the music, the improvisations were informed by the melodies as opposed to all of these chord progressions, the melodies. Steve Wilson, I was over at DePaul University working with some students over there but Steve Wilson, a great saxophonist came in and gave a master class that was awesome. And he talks about when he first came to New York that he came to a jam session with all of the older cats from the Ellington — older cats — survivors that had played with Duke’s band. And he asked them, he says, so tell me something — because he wanted to know how Duke worked with the musicians. And the cats told him, the cats told him that Duke would like sometimes write the person’s name on the chart. So then Steve then asked them well when it came to soloing how did Duke write out the chord changes. And the answer was, “Chord changes!” They said no you have to listen to whatever the melody was and you have to figure that out from that. So they weren’t sitting down looking at like minor 2-5s. The melody informed the improvisation. So you had to know the melody. And all those great, great, great solos from, from, from the swing era, those solos were — people understood, they understood the melodies. Now of course you have geniuses like Coleman Hawkins who’s going to do what he did like “Body and Soul” where he starts introducing basically sheets of sound and that whole other approach of stuff. Now was he playing by ear? Did he have great ears? I don’t know. I don’t know if he was understanding the chord progressions. I know that he was definitely looking to something a little bit different. I know Dizzy played with him so a lot of cats went forward and started to try some other things. But I think it was Bird that was talking about this, through some friends of mine that dealt with Bird, some friends of mine from Seattle that are already gone but that knew Bird and how Bird told them I had to learn how to play all of these different things, whether it was the blues, “Rhythm” changes, “Cherokee” and something else in all twelve keys. And he goes by the time we know,

we’re just playing by ear. They’re playing by ear. I mean they understand the chord changes most definitely. And I think it’s important for us to learn it, but in the event of a person who’s learning it by ear how do I explain how Stan Getz can play on all of those Chick Corea tunes on that recording “Captain Marvel” when he didn’t know how to read chord changes. And you could hear it, you could hear. Sometimes he deals with things in a certain way. Same thing with Chet Baker. I mean all of those recordings of “Have You Met Miss Jones” by Chet Baker, they’re not really good. I’ve got to tell you something, because Chet always took that bridge that has like those Giant Stepy kind of things. And he never got it right. He never got it right. So you know, I’m sorry, and I love Chet mind you. My record collection, I have a lot of Woody and, as far as trumpets, Woody and Freddie and Dizzy. But man I got tons of Chet because there was something special about Chet. I loved Chet, Blue Mitchell, Art Farmer. I like the cats that played the pretty stuff. I like Donald Byrd. I like those cats. They play real pretty.
